Own it: Mars is a free, open educational web game where kids ages 7–15 run a Martian outpost and learn that every decision has a consequence. Players tap a map to visit the Habitat, Greenhouse, Solar Panels, Robot Garage, and Expedition, manage six resources (energy, food, equipment, health, time, and data), and launch the ship home. Random, timed events, such as solar and dust storms, force quick choices with uncertain outcomes. After each decision, the game explains the real science behind it, citing NASA/JPL and Canadian Space Agency sources, and a final mission log shows what the player protected and what it cost.

It addresses the challenge by letting young people experience the real trade-offs of running a Mars outpost instead of just reading about them. It matters because science education in Mexico needs new tools: in PISA 2025, Mexico ranked 37th of 38 OECD countries in science. Own it: Mars builds critical thinking, decision-making, and curiosity, runs in any browser with no account or install.
details:
Project Details
Team PioNotFound · NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026

What does it do and how does it work?
Own it: Mars is a free, open educational web game where kids run a small outpost on Mars and learn, by playing, that every decision has a consequence. It is built for children ages 7 to 15, and also for teachers and families. It can be played in a classroom or at home from a simple link, with no account and nothing to install.

The player is in charge of a Martian base. A tap map shows five places: the Habitat, the Greenhouse, the Solar Panels, the Robot Garage and the Expedition, plus the Spaceship that waits for the final mission. At each place, the player reads a short story and chooses one of several options. Six meters track the base: Energy, Food, Equipment, Health, Time and Data. Every option changes the meters in a different way, and many include a chance that something goes wrong. For example, servicing every system in the Habitat costs energy and time but keeps the base safe. Skipping maintenance saves resources but risks a failure in life support, the computers or communications.

The places connect to each other, so choices echo. The Expedition, where the player collects radiation data on the surface, only opens if the base has enough Food, and Food can only be produced in the Greenhouse. The player can go back for the radiation suit, which takes time and costs resources, or stay without protection and risk losing everything. Back at the base, the Laboratory lets the player analyze the data fast, using little energy but with a chance of losing it all, or carefully, using more energy but keeping every piece. Then the results are sent to Earth.

On top of that, the game throws sudden, timed events. A solar storm or a dust storm can arrive at a random moment, at the start of the game or right after any task. A pop-up appears over the map with a countdown, and the player has a few seconds to choose. For the solar storm: disconnect everything and lose the food in the freezer, stay connected and risk the equipment, or disconnect only the science equipment and lose data. If time runs out, the base does nothing, and that is a decision with consequences too. No option is the right answer.

After every decision, the game shows what changed in the meters and opens a panel called “Is this real? The science behind it”. It explains the real science behind the situation and links to the official source, from NASA/JPL-Caltech or the Canadian Space Agency. For example, the solar storm event is based on a real storm that reached Mars in September 2017. It lit up an aurora 25 times brighter than normal and doubled the radiation measured on the surface. The dust storm event is based on NASA’s report about the Opportunity rover, which suspended its science because it runs on sunlight, while Curiosity, with a nuclear-powered battery, was largely unaffected.

The game ends in one of three ways:

  • The ship launches: if the five base tasks are done and no key meter is empty, the player launches the ship and sees a mission log with two lists, what you protected and what it cost.
  • Game over: if Health reaches zero, the game explains the real radiation risk, asks “What would you protect first next time?”, and the player can try again.
  • A fresh start: if the ship can no longer launch (for example, the fast lab analysis wiped all the data), the game detects the dead end and offers a new start, so nobody gets stuck.

Because events are random and many outcomes depend on chance, every game is different.

What benefits does it have?

  • For students: it practices critical thinking, decision-making under uncertainty and time pressure, curiosity and scientific knowledge, all together. Instead of memorizing facts about space, kids experience the trade-offs that mission planners face: you cannot protect everything, and you must live with the result. The game never labels a choice as “wrong”, and the end-of-game log invites reflection instead of giving a score. Failure is part of learning.
  • For teachers and families: it is free, works on phones, tablets and computers, and needs no registration, installation or setup. The whole game is one file that also runs offline, which helps schools with limited connectivity. A session is short, so it fits in a class period, and it gives teachers a natural conversation starter: “What did you protect, and what did it cost?”
  • For trust and safety: all science content is curated from official sources and credited inside the game, so teachers don’t need to verify it. The game collects no personal data and has no accounts or tracking. The only thing it stores in the browser is whether the sound is muted.
  • For sustainability: it is a static website, so it needs no servers or database. The annual maintenance budget is about 384 USD, and volunteers could cut it in half.

What is the intended impact?
Mexican students are lagging in science. In PISA 2025, Mexico ranked 37th of the 38 OECD countries in science, and about half of its students did not reach the basic level of proficiency, compared with about a quarter on average across the OECD. Part of the problem is how space and science are taught. Children know about rockets and astronauts, but not about the decisions behind a mission, and the content they find is either too simple to challenge them or too technical to follow.

Own it: Mars aims to close that gap by making the decision-making side of space exploration approachable, interactive and fun. We want more children to become curious about science and space, to understand that real missions are made of trade-offs, and to build the habit of asking “what does this decision cost, and what does it protect?” That habit applies far beyond Mars.

We want to measure that impact honestly. Our plan is a pilot with a small group of students and their teachers, using supervised activities. We will look at how many participants complete the mission and how their answers to knowledge questions change before and after playing, without collecting unnecessary personal data. The game has not been tested with children yet, and its numbers (chances, costs and timers) are design values that we will tune with playtesting. Pilot results are also what foundations ask for when they consider educational funding.

Looking forward, the project is designed to grow. New missions and events can be added as long as each one has an official source, and the game could be translated and adapted for other classrooms and countries.

What tools, coding languages, hardware or software did you use?

  • Prototype: we first built the game in Twine 2 with the Harlowe story format, using HTML and CSS for the layout and styling. This let us quickly test the decisions, the consequences and the balance of the six meters before writing the final game.
  • Web version: we then turned the prototype into a full web game in plain JavaScript (ES modules), HTML and CSS, with no external game engine or framework, with help from Claude, an AI assistant by Anthropic. Claude helped us port the rules to code and write the tests and the build script. Our team made the design decisions, wrote the game’s rules and story, and reviewed the results. The game logic (meters, rules, random events and probabilities) is a separate engine with no graphics, so it can be tested on its own. The interface (tap map, pop-up windows, meters bar and event pop-ups) runs in the browser.
  • Visuals and sound: all drawings (stations, map, rocket and icons) are inline SVG made in code. Sound effects (tap, event alarm, a neutral chime after each choice, failure and launch sounds) are generated with the Web Audio API. The font is Baloo 2 from Google Fonts, under the SIL Open Font License.
  • Music: our background song, “Alone in Space with Only Your Descriptions”, was composed and produced by our team in FL Studio.
  • Development and testing: Node.js runs our automated checks (npm test): rule checks for the engine and 2,000 random playthroughs that confirm every game can end and nobody gets stuck. A small build script produces a single self-contained HTML file (about 1.9 MB, with the music inside) that works offline, by double-click, or on any static host.
  • Hosting and collaboration: the code lives in a GitHub repository, and the game is published for free on GitHub Pages. With the current file size, GitHub Pages can serve around 50,000 plays per month, and we documented when and how to move to another static host if the game grows.
  • Hardware: no special hardware. We developed and tested on regular computers, and the game runs in any modern browser (Chrome, Edge, Firefox or Safari) on phones, tablets and computers.
  • Science sources: NASA/JPL-Caltech articles and photojournal pages, and Canadian Space Agency resources provided by the challenge, listed in the repository’s credits and shown inside the game.

How is your project creative?

  • It teaches the decision, not just the fact. Most space games for kids test skills or share facts. Own it: Mars puts the player in the seat of a mission planner. Every option protects one thing and risks another, and the game deliberately has no perfect answer. Even the sound design supports this: after each choice a soft, neutral chime plays, so no choice “sounds like a mistake”.
  • Visual storytelling. Kids live one day as the leader of a Mars base, and a colorful map, pop-up missions and live meters show what every choice changes.
  • Real science appears at the moment it matters. The “Is this real?” panel opens right after the consequence, when the child is most curious about why it happened, and it always shows the source. The solar storm and the dust storm are real events from NASA reports, turned into playable decisions.
  • Systems that connect. The Expedition depends on the Greenhouse, the lab depends on the Expedition, and the launch depends on the whole base. Kids discover for themselves that in a real outpost, food, energy, equipment, time and data are linked.
  • Uncertainty and time pressure. Random storms with a countdown, probabilities on risky options and a default consequence when the timer runs out recreate the feeling of deciding with incomplete information. It is exciting but not punishing, and each game is different.
  • A reflective ending. Instead of a score, the mission log shows what the player protected and what it cost, and the end screens ask what they would protect next time. Winning and losing become a conversation.
  • Our own art and music. The map and places are drawn in SVG code, the sound effects are generated in code, and the soundtrack is our own song made in FL Studio. This also keeps the game small, free of image licenses and able to work offline.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Audience and clarity: we designed for ages 7 to 15, so texts are short and simple, with each science term explained in a sentence. The meters bar and the tap map keep the interface simple, and decisions fit in a pop-up so the game never overwhelms a child.
  • Scientific accuracy and honesty: every science statement comes from an official source and is credited inside the game. We separate real science from game design: chances, costs and timers are design values, not NASA data, and the game never presents curated text as live data. Part of the Canadian Space Agency content describes the International Space Station, and we use it to explain principles that also apply to future missions.
  • Privacy and safety for children: no accounts, no tracking and no data collection. The only thing stored in the browser is whether the sound is muted.
  • Access and equity: it works on phones, tablets and computers, needs no installation, runs offline as a single file, and is free. This matters for schools with limited devices or connectivity.
  • Fair and healthy design: we avoided punishing the player. Game Over explains the real risk and invites another try, dead ends are detected so nobody gets stuck, and the timer has a clear default. Sound starts only after the first tap, the volume is low by default and the mute button is always visible. We also simplified the game to a single day and replaced hunger and thirst with a food requirement for the Expedition, to keep it focused and not stressful.
  • Responsible use of AI: we used Claude as a coding assistant and were transparent about it. The game design, rules, story and music are our team’s work, and we reviewed and tested everything it produced.
  • Quality and testing: we built a Twine prototype first, then automated tests, including thousands of random playthroughs, so the rules are consistent. We are open about what is still missing: playtesting with real students to tune the numbers, and a Spanish version, a natural next step for a project aimed at Mexican classrooms.
  • Sustainability and business model: the game is free for students. Its upkeep would be financed with business sponsorships and educational grants, with volunteers to reduce costs, following precedents such as Fundación RobotiX and Fundación BBVA in Mexico, and open projects like The Odin Project and the Processing Foundation. The annual maintenance budget is about 384 USD: four quarterly maintenance services at 80 USD each, plus a 64 USD contingency reserve. With 50% volunteer help, it drops to 192 USD. We don’t have confirmed funding yet: these are precedents and a plan, and our next step is a pilot that shows students learn.
  • Intellectual property: the music is our own, the art and sound effects were made in code for this project, and all science content is credited to its source. The repository lists every asset, its author and its license.
  • Time and scope: with limited hackathon time, we focused on a playable, stable prototype with the essential decisions, the real science and a clear ending, rather than many unfinished features.
